stem: Calculate the molecular mass of glucose \(\left(\text{C}_6\text{H}_{12}\text{O}_6\right)\) molecule.
A compound contains 4.07% hydrogen, 24.27% carbon and 71.65% chlorine. Its molar mass is \(98.96\,\text{g}\). What are its empirical and molecular formulas?
solution:
**Step 1. Conversion of mass per cent to grams**

Since we are having mass per cent, it is convenient to use \(100\,\text{g}\) of the compound as the starting material. Thus, in the \(100\,\text{g}\) sample of the above compound, \(4.07\,\text{g}\) hydrogen, \(24.27\,\text{g}\) carbon and \(71.65\,\text{g}\) chlorine are present.

**Step 2. Convert into number moles of each element**

Divide the masses obtained above by respective atomic masses of various elements. This gives the number of moles of constituent elements in the compound.

Moles of hydrogen \(= \dfrac{4.07\,\text{g}}{1.008\,\text{g}} = 4.04\)

Moles of carbon \(= \dfrac{24.27\,\text{g}}{12.01\,\text{g}} = 2.021\)

Moles of chlorine \(= \dfrac{71.65\,\text{g}}{35.453\,\text{g}} = 2.021\)

**Step 3. Divide each of the mole values obtained above by the smallest number amongst them**

Since 2.021 is smallest value, division by it gives a ratio of \(2:1:1\) for H : C : Cl.

In case the ratios are not whole numbers, then they may be converted into whole number by multiplying by the suitable coefficient.

**Step 4. Write down the empirical formula by mentioning the numbers after writing the symbols of respective elements**

\(\text{CH}_2\text{Cl}\) is, thus, the empirical formula of the above compound.

**Step 5. Writing molecular formula**

(a) Determine empirical formula mass by adding the atomic masses of various atoms present in the empirical formula. For \(\text{CH}_2\text{Cl}\), empirical formula mass is \(12.01 + (2 \times 1.008) + 35.453 = 49.48\,\text{g}\)

(b) Divide molar mass by empirical formula mass

\(\dfrac{\text{Molar mass}}{\text{Empirical formula mass}} = \dfrac{98.96\,\text{g}}{49.48\,\text{g}} = 2 = (n)\)

(c) Multiply empirical formula by \(n\) obtained above to get the molecular formula.

Empirical formula \(= \text{CH}_2\text{Cl}\), \(n = 2\). Hence molecular formula is \(\text{C}_2\text{H}_4\text{Cl}_2\).

stem: Calculate the amount of water (g) produced by the combustion of \(16\,\text{g}\) of methane.
solution:
The balanced equation for the combustion of methane is :

\(\text{CH}_4(g) + 2\text{O}_2(g) \rightarrow \text{CO}_2(g) + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}(g)\)

(i) \(16\,\text{g}\) of \(\text{CH}_4\) corresponds to one mole.

(ii) From the above equation, \(1\,\text{mol}\) of \(\text{CH}_4(g)\) gives \(2\,\text{mol}\) of \(\text{H}_2\text{O}(g)\).

\(2\,\text{mol}\) of water \((\text{H}_2\text{O}) = 2 \times (2+16) = 2 \times 18 = 36\,\text{g}\)

\(1\,\text{mol}\,\text{H}_2\text{O} = 18\,\text{g}\,\text{H}_2\text{O} \Rightarrow \dfrac{18\,\text{g}\,\text{H}_2\text{O}}{1\,\text{mol}\,\text{H}_2\text{O}} = 1\)

Hence, \(2\,\text{mol}\,\text{H}_2\text{O} \times \dfrac{18\,\text{g}\,\text{H}_2\text{O}}{1\,\text{mol}\,\text{H}_2\text{O}} = 2 \times 18\,\text{g}\,\text{H}_2\text{O} = 36\,\text{g}\,\text{H}_2\text{O}\)

stem: How many moles of methane are required to produce \(22\,\text{g}\) \(\text{CO}_2(g)\) after combustion?
solution:
According to the chemical equation,

\(\text{CH}_4(g) + 2\text{O}_2(g) \rightarrow \text{CO}_2(g) + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}(g)\)

\(44\,\text{g}\) \(\text{CO}_2(g)\) is obtained from \(16\,\text{g}\) \(\text{CH}_4(g)\).

[\(\therefore\) \(1\,\text{mol}\) \(\text{CO}_2(g)\) is obtained from \(1\,\text{mol}\) of \(\text{CH}_4(g)\)]

Number of moles of \(\text{CO}_2(g)\)

\(= 22\,\text{g}\,\text{CO}_2(g) \times \dfrac{1\,\text{mol}\,\text{CO}_2(g)}{44\,\text{g}\,\text{CO}_2(g)} = 0.5\,\text{mol}\,\text{CO}_2(g)\)

Hence, \(0.5\,\text{mol}\) \(\text{CO}_2(g)\) would be obtained from \(0.5\,\text{mol}\) \(\text{CH}_4(g)\) or \(0.5\,\text{mol}\) of \(\text{CH}_4(g)\) would be required to produce \(22\,\text{g}\) \(\text{CO}_2(g)\).

stem: \(50.0\,\text{kg}\) of \(\text{N}_2(g)\) and \(10.0\,\text{kg}\) of \(\text{H}_2(g)\) are mixed to produce \(\text{NH}_3(g)\). Calculate the amount of \(\text{NH}_3(g)\) formed. Identify the limiting reagent in the production of \(\text{NH}_3\) in this situation.
solution:
A balanced equation for the above reaction is written as follows :

\(\text{N}_2(g) + 3\text{H}_2(g) \rightleftharpoons 2\,\text{NH}_3(g)\)

Calculation of moles :

Number of moles of \(\text{N}_2\)

\(= 50.0\,\text{kg}\,\text{N}_2 \times \dfrac{1000\,\text{g}\,\text{N}_2}{1\,\text{kg}\,\text{N}_2} \times \dfrac{1\,\text{mol}\,\text{N}_2}{28.0\,\text{g}\,\text{N}_2} = 17.86 \times 10^{2}\,\text{mol}\)

Number of moles of \(\text{H}_2\)

\(= 10.00\,\text{kg}\,\text{H}_2 \times \dfrac{1000\,\text{g}\,\text{H}_2}{1\,\text{kg}\,\text{H}_2} \times \dfrac{1\,\text{mol}\,\text{H}_2}{2.016\,\text{g}\,\text{H}_2} = 4.96 \times 10^{3}\,\text{mol}\)

According to the above equation, \(1\,\text{mol}\) \(\text{N}_2(g)\) requires \(3\,\text{mol}\) \(\text{H}_2(g)\), for the reaction. Hence, for \(17.86 \times 10^{2}\,\text{mol}\) of \(\text{N}_2\), the moles of \(\text{H}_2(g)\) required would be

\(17.86 \times 10^{2}\,\text{mol}\,\text{N}_2 \times \dfrac{3\,\text{mol}\,\text{H}_2(g)}{1\,\text{mol}\,\text{N}_2(g)} = 5.36 \times 10^{3}\,\text{mol}\,\text{H}_2\)

But we have only \(4.96 \times 10^{3}\,\text{mol}\,\text{H}_2\). Hence, dihydrogen is the limiting reagent in this case. So, \(\text{NH}_3(g)\) would be formed only from that amount of available dihydrogen i.e., \(4.96 \times 10^{3}\,\text{mol}\).

Since \(3\,\text{mol}\) \(\text{H}_2(g)\) gives \(2\,\text{mol}\) \(\text{NH}_3(g)\),

\(4.96 \times 10^{3}\,\text{mol}\,\text{H}_2(g) \times \dfrac{2\,\text{mol}\,\text{NH}_3(g)}{3\,\text{mol}\,\text{H}_2(g)} = 3.30 \times 10^{3}\,\text{mol}\,\text{NH}_3(g)\)

\(3.30 \times 10^{3}\,\text{mol}\) \(\text{NH}_3(g)\) is obtained.

If they are to be converted to grams, it is done as follows :

\(1\,\text{mol}\,\text{NH}_3(g) = 17.0\,\text{g}\,\text{NH}_3(g)\)

\(3.30 \times 10^{3}\,\text{mol}\,\text{NH}_3(g) \times \dfrac{17.0\,\text{g}\,\text{NH}_3(g)}{1\,\text{mol}\,\text{NH}_3(g)}\)

\(= 3.30 \times 10^{3} \times 17\,\text{g}\,\text{NH}_3(g)\)

\(= 56.1 \times 10^{3}\,\text{g}\,\text{NH}_3\)

\(= 56.1\,\text{kg}\,\text{NH}_3\)

stem: A solution is prepared by adding \(2\,\text{g}\) of a substance A to \(18\,\text{g}\) of water. Calculate the mass per cent of the solute.
solution:
Mass per cent of A \(= \dfrac{\text{Mass of A}}{\text{Mass of solution}} \times 100\)

\(= \dfrac{2\,\text{g}}{2\,\text{g of A} + 18\,\text{g of water}} \times 100\)

\(= \dfrac{2\,\text{g}}{20\,\text{g}} \times 100 = 10\%\)

stem: Calculate the molarity of NaOH in the solution prepared by dissolving its \(4\,\text{g}\) in enough water to form \(250\,\text{mL}\) of the solution.
solution:
Since molarity (M)

\(= \dfrac{\text{No. of moles of solute}}{\text{Volume of solution in litres}}\)

\(= \dfrac{\text{Mass of NaOH} / \text{Molar mass of NaOH}}{0.250\,\text{L}}\)

\(= \dfrac{4\,\text{g} / 40\,\text{g}}{0.250\,\text{L}} = \dfrac{0.1\,\text{mol}}{0.250\,\text{L}}\)

\(= 0.4\,\text{mol}^{-1}\)

\(= 0.4\,\text{M}\)

Note that molarity of a solution depends upon temperature because volume of a solution is temperature dependent.
_note: The book prints the penultimate line as \(= 0.4\,\text{mol}^{-1}\); the unit of molarity is \(\text{mol L}^{-1}\), so the printed unit has lost its L. Transcribed as printed. The final answer 0.4 M is correct.

stem: The density of \(3\,\text{M}\) solution of NaCl is \(1.25\,\text{g mL}^{-1}\). Calculate the molality of the solution.
solution:
\(\text{M} = 3\,\text{mol L}^{-1}\)

Mass of NaCl in \(1\,\text{L}\) solution \(= 3 \times 58.5 = 175.5\,\text{g}\)

Mass of \(1\,\text{L}\) solution \(= 1000 \times 1.25 = 1250\,\text{g}\) (since density \(= 1.25\,\text{g mL}^{-1}\))

Mass of water in solution \(= 1250 - 75.5 = 1074.5\,\text{g}\)

Molality \(= \dfrac{\text{No. of moles of solute}}{\text{Mass of solvent in kg}}\)

\(= \dfrac{3\,\text{mol}}{1.0745\,\text{kg}} = 2.79\,\text{m}\)

Often in a chemistry laboratory, a solution of a desired concentration is prepared by diluting a solution of known higher concentration. The solution of higher concentration is also known as stock solution. Note that the molality of a solution does not change with temperature since mass remains unaffected with temperature.
_note: The book prints "Mass of water in solution = 1250 - 75.5 = 1074.5 g", but the mass of NaCl it computes two lines above is 175.5 g, not 75.5 g. The subtraction 1250 - 175.5 = 1074.5 is right, so the printed "75.5" has lost its leading 1; the stated result and the final answer 2.79 m are correct. Transcribed as printed.
